query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing approximately 10–20 at.% of Mo with V in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will reduce the alloy’s overall electronegativity difference, which in turn modifies the solute–dislocation interactions to promote easier dislocation motion and improved plasticity without a significant loss in compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa and limited plasticity.
generation.intervention: Substitute about 10–20 at.% of Mo with vanadium (V) while keeping the other elemental proportions equiatomic.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compressive testing; the alloy must maintain its disordered BCC structure and overall phase stability; the substitution range is strictly between 10 and 20 at.%.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified local solute-induced strain fields and reduced electronegativity gradients that affect dislocation pinning and mobility.
generation.mechanism: Lower Mo content decreases the electronegativity mismatch, thereby reducing the pinning effect on dislocations. Vanadium, having a lower electronegativity and similar atomic size, preserves solid-solution strengthening while facilitating more effective dislocation glide, leading to enhanced ductility alongside maintained yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with 10–20 at.% Mo replaced by V is expected to show a room-temperature compressive yield strength similar to the original (~1719 MPa) while exhibiting an increased plastic strain (improved work-hardening and ductility), compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo without any Mo-to-V substitution.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated only if the Mo replacement is maintained within 10–20 at.%. Substitutions outside this range might either insufficiently reduce the electronegativity difference (if below 10 at.%) or degrade the solid-solution strengthening and phase stability (if above 20 at.%).
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in plasticity and the potential trade-off with strength remain uncertain and may depend on subtle atomic-level interactions. Further experimental validation is needed to confirm the optimal substitution level.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of alloys with controlled Mo-to-V substitutions at 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30% in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo system. Use X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to confirm retention of the disordered BCC phase. Perform room-temperature compressive tests to measure yield strength, plastic strain to failure, and work-hardening behavior.
measurements: Phase verification via XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with 10–20 at.% Mo replacement by V do not exhibit a noticeable increase in plasticity (e.g., higher strain-to-failure or improved work-hardening behavior) without a significant reduction (greater than ~10%) in compressive yield strength compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.2. Non-Monotonic Change of the Strain-Hardening Behavior with V Addition
cited_evidence.text: The strain-hardening rate of 2V alloys decreases rapidly at the beginning of deformation due to recovery. Subsequently, the strain-hardening rate levels off and then decreases slowly. This strain-hardening behavior can be related to the low SFE of the 2V alloy. Full dislocations are prone to dissociate into Shockley partial dislocations on {111} slip planes, forming SFs during the plastic deformation process []. These SFs are supposed to impede dislocation motion and induce a strong strain-hardening effect, retaining the high strain-hardening rate and forming the plateau. With a further increase in tensile strain, the local stress reaches the critical value for deformation-induced phase transformation, and thin HCP lamellae are activated [,], which can effectively impede dislocation motion []. During the deformation process, nano-sized HCP lamellae are alternately arranged, which relieves the local stress concentration of the alloy and delays the necking process []. These high-density dislocations, SFs, and HCP phases act synergistically to improve the strain-hardening ability of the alloy. The SFE of the alloy increases with V addition. cited_evidence.kind: web:Electronegativity difference versus ideal mixing entropy in 3d CCAs
cited_evidence.text: There are several interesting points in diagram Fig. 4a. First, in spite of its lower chemical complexity, CrCoNi (Δχ = 0.100) has a higher solid-solution strengthening than CrMnFeCoNi (Δχ = 0.080). This is consistent with a previous observation that CrCoNi exhibits higher yield strength than CrMnFeCoNi. Second, FeMn, basis for many commercially used iron-manganese steels, is located at a very low position (Δχ ≈ 0.020). This implies good potential to develop a 3d CCA with very high strength if we optimize the plasticity mechanisms of CCA with high Δχ. Third, mixing entropy, one of the key properties of HEAs (a subclass of CCAs), is not strongly correlated with the electronegativity difference and thus with high solid-solution strengthening per se. Furthermore, there is a region in which the mixing entropy should be decreased to obtain greater solid-solution strengthening effects. Mixing entropy does not include information about the difference among the constituting elements, i.e., differences in local atomic configurations. cited_evidence.text: To further cement that the edge dislocations can control the strength, we apply a new theory for the yield strength versus temperature and strain rate for edge dislocations moving through a random BCC alloy. In the theory, each alloying element is viewed as a solute that interacts with a dislocation in a hypothetical homogeneous “average” alloy that has all the macroscopic properties of the true random alloy. Fluctuations in the local arrangements of solutes create large local variations in the potential energy for the dislocation. The dislocation thus spontaneously adopts a low-energy wavy structure to take advantage of the low-energy solute environments and avoid the high-energy environments. The plastic flow then requires the temperature- and stress-assisted thermal activation of the dislocations out of the low-energy environments and over the large barriers created by the adjacent high-energy environments along the glide plane in the random alloy.
